newsitem.title: CANADA: Inco seeks mediator help to resolve strike.
newsitem.headline: Inco seeks mediator help to resolve strike.

text.p: Inco Ltd said on Tuesday that it was seeking the help of a provincial mediator to help resolve a strike at its Sudbury operations.

Inco spokesman David Allen said the company had not sought a formal mediation process from the Ontario Ministry of Labor, but would like the mediation officer to return to the table and help facilitate talks between the nickel-producing giant and its Sudbury operations union.

"The matter is in the hands of the mediator," Allen told Reuters. "The mediator met both parties a few days ago and determined there was no point in him playing any further role and he withdrew. We are endeavoring to arrange his return to the process."
Spokesmen for the United Steelworkers of America told Reuters on Monday that the union suspected Inco had asked for mediation.

"The news media is saying that Inco has been in contact with the provincial mediator and that something might happen on Wednesday, but nobody has told us," said David Campbell, President of Local 6500 of the United Steelworkers of America. "It's been in the papers, on television and radio."
Campbell said the union is waiting to be contacted by Inco in the event that the company would like to revive negotiations.
"We're ready to roll when they're ready," he said.
Inco's 4,670 unionized Sudbury workers went on strike at midnight on Monday, June 2, after voting 60.4 percent against a contract offer endorsed by union leaders.
Union officials said that Inco is likely to make a push to resove the dispute before its summer shutdown period, which begins in July.
"I think there is going to be an effort to end this thing before June," said Wayne Fraser Sudbury spokesman for the union. "If that doesn't happen I think we're looking at late summer or early fall."
According to Inco's 1997 production plan, the Ontario division was expected to produce about 230 million pounds of nickel, about 200 million pounds of copper and about four million pounds of cobalt.

Inco's Port Colborne, Ontario refinery, which processes cobalt, precious metals and electro-nickel, was not affected by the Sudbury strike. Unionized workers at the refinery approved the contract on Monday, June 2.
